q: How does NestJS relate to Express and Fastify?
options: It replaces them with its own HTTP server written in TypeScript
It is a plugin you register inside an Express or Fastify app
It adds modules, a DI container and request slots, and runs on Express or Fastify through an adapter
It only works with Express; Fastify needs a separate framework
explain: NestJS is an application framework: it provides structure and delegates HTTP to an adapter (@nestjs/platform-express by default, @nestjs/platform-fastify on request). It is not a plugin inside those frameworks, and the Fastify adapter is official.

q: Where should the rule "only a paid order can be cancelled" live?
options: In the use case, which throws a domain error that the HTTP layer maps to 409
In the controller, next to the status code it produces
In the repository, as a condition of the UPDATE query only
In a guard, so the handler never runs for unpaid orders
explain: Business rules belong to the use case so every caller (controller, queue consumer, test) applies them. A guard is for authentication and authorisation, not for business state; a conditional update can back the rule up, but the rule and its error belong to the use case.

q: In ports and adapters, what is a port?
options: The TCP port the HTTP server listens on
An interface declared by the core (for example OrderRepository) describing what it needs from the outside
A class that implements a database query
A Nest module that exports a service
explain: A port is owned by the application core and names a capability it needs; adapters such as a Postgres repository implement it. The class with the SQL is the adapter, not the port, which is why the core never imports a driver.

q: What is a composition root?
options: The root module that every NestJS app must declare
A base class that all services extend to receive dependencies
A global registry that any file can query for a dependency
The one place, run once at startup, that creates the concrete adapters and passes them to the code that needs them
explain: The composition root builds the object graph explicitly, for example buildApp(config) creating the pool, the repository and the use case. A global registry queried from anywhere is the service locator pattern, which hides dependencies instead of passing them in.

q: A Nest service needs an OrderRepository, which is a TypeScript interface. Why does it need @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY)?
options: Interfaces do not exist at runtime, so Nest cannot resolve them from the parameter type and needs a token
Because @Inject makes the provider request-scoped
Because Nest can only inject classes from the same module without it
Because the decorator turns the interface into an abstract class
explain: Nest reads constructor parameter types recorded by emitDecoratorMetadata; an interface is erased by the compiler, so there is nothing to look up. A Symbol or string token registered with { provide: TOKEN, useClass: … } fills the gap. @Inject has no effect on scope.

q: What is the default scope of a Nest provider?
options: One instance per request
One instance per module that imports it
One instance for the whole application (singleton)
A new instance for each consumer (transient)
explain: Providers are singletons unless declared otherwise. Scope.REQUEST and Scope.TRANSIENT are opt-in, and request scope spreads to every consumer, which is why singletons with a context store are preferred.

q: In which order do these run for a successful request in NestJS?
options: Middleware, pipe, guard, interceptor, handler
Middleware, guard, interceptor, pipe, handler
Guard, middleware, pipe, interceptor, handler
Middleware, interceptor, guard, pipe, handler
explain: The Nest docs and a measurement on Nest 12.3.2 agree: middleware, guards, interceptors (before), pipes, then the handler, then interceptors on the way out. Guards come before pipes, so an unauthenticated request is rejected before its body is validated.

q: On Nest 12, how do you validate a request body with a Zod schema without an extra library?
options: Call schema.parse(body) inside every handler
Wrap the schema with createZodDto and use ValidationPipe
Add class-validator decorators generated from the schema
Write @Body({ schema: CreateOrderSchema }) and register StandardSchemaValidationPipe
explain: Nest 12 accepts any Standard Schema library on @Body, @Query and @Param, and StandardSchemaValidationPipe validates those parameters. createZodDto comes from the separate nestjs-zod library and pairs with its own ZodValidationPipe, not with class-validator's ValidationPipe.

q: In the old Express 5 server.ts, an async route throws after an await, and a four-parameter error handler is registered last. What happens?
options: The process crashes with an unhandled rejection
The request hangs until the client times out
Express sends its default HTML 500 page
The error reaches the error handler, which answers with the mapped response
explain: Express 5 passes a rejected promise from a handler to next(err). Measured on Express 5.3.0: this route's error reached the handler, which answered a 404 Problem Details. The hang or crash happened in Express 4 without a wrapper such as express-async-errors.

q: The config schema reads FEATURE_REFUNDS: z.coerce.boolean() and the environment has FEATURE_REFUNDS=false. What is the value?
options: true, because any non-empty string is truthy
false
A validation error at startup
undefined, so the default applies
explain: Measured on Zod 4.6.7: z.coerce.boolean().parse('false') returns true, since coercion is Boolean('false'). z.stringbool() reads "false", "0", "no" and "off" as false and rejects unknown words.

q: What does AsyncLocalStorage.run(store, fn) give a service?
options: A cache shared by all requests for the lifetime of the process
Access to store from any code started by fn, across awaits, and from nothing else
A new worker thread with its own copy of store
A way to make a Nest provider request-scoped
explain: The store follows the asynchronous work started inside run, so each request sees its own request id even when many are interleaved. It is not shared across requests (that would be a module variable), and it is what lets Nest code avoid request scope (nestjs-cls is built on it).

q: A Kubernetes pod receives SIGTERM. What should the service do first?
options: Close the database pool so no new queries start
Call process.exit(0); Kubernetes restarts the work elsewhere
Stop listening immediately so no request arrives after the signal
Keep serving while failing the readiness probe, and wait a few seconds for endpoint removal to propagate
explain: Kubernetes removes the pod from endpoints at the same time as it sends SIGTERM, so new requests can still arrive briefly; closing the listener at once turns them into errors. Closing the pool first breaks the requests still in flight.

q: Besides the Orders API, the team must ship a small endpoint for the delivery partner that runs as a Cloudflare Worker and also, for local development, on Node. Which framework fits best?
options: NestJS with the Fastify adapter
Express 5
Hono, which is built on Web-standard Request and Response and runs on Workers and on Node
Fastify 5 with its serverless mode
explain: Hono's documentation lists Cloudflare Workers, Deno, Bun, AWS Lambda and Node (through its Node adapter) because it only uses Web standards. Express and Fastify are built on Node's http module, and NestJS adds a heavy build and container that a small edge function does not need.

q: A NestJS app registers a global guard, interceptor, pipe and exception filter that each log their name. OrdersService.get throws OrderNotFoundError, which the filter handles. What is logged?
options: middleware > guard > interceptor:before > pipe > handler > service > interceptor:error > filter
middleware > guard > pipe > interceptor:before > handler > service > filter > interceptor:error
middleware > interceptor:before > guard > pipe > handler > service > filter
middleware > guard > interceptor:before > pipe > handler > service > filter
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2 with the Fastify adapter: the interceptor wraps the handler as an RxJS stream, so it sees the error before the filter turns it into a response. The tempting last option forgets that interceptors are on the error path too, which matters when an interceptor maps or logs errors.

q: A singleton TenantContext provider was changed to Scope.REQUEST to hold the current tenant. OrdersController injects it. What happens to the controller?
options: Nothing: controllers are always singletons
It is constructed again for every request, as is every provider in the chain that depends on TenantContext
Nest refuses to start because controllers cannot depend on request-scoped providers
It keeps the instance created for the first request
explain: Request scope bubbles up the injection chain (Nest docs). Measured on Nest 12.3.2: a controller injecting a request-scoped provider was constructed twice for two requests. Storing the tenant with nestjs-cls keeps everything singleton.

q: A Fastify 5 service has no setErrorHandler. A handler fails with new Error('connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432'). What does the client receive?
options: A 500 whose JSON body contains "message":"connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432"
A 500 with a generic "Internal Server Error" message only
A 502 Bad Gateway, since the database is unreachable
The connection is reset without a response
explain: Measured on Fastify 5.12.7: {"statusCode":500,"error":"Internal Server Error","message":"connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432"}. The generic body is what NestJS does by default, not Fastify; a custom error handler that maps through toProblem and logs the details is required.

q: A Fastify 5 service calls await app.close() on SIGTERM. One request is in flight on a keep-alive connection and finishes 300 ms later. Default settings. When does close() resolve?
options: Right after the in-flight response is sent
Immediately: close() destroys every connection
Never, until Kubernetes sends SIGKILL
About 72 seconds later, when the idle keep-alive connection times out
explain: Measured on Fastify 5.12.7: close() resolved after 73 s, because the connection stayed open after its response until Fastify's 72 000 ms keepAliveTimeout. Sending Connection: close on responses during the shutdown brought it to 41 ms; in Kubernetes the 30 s grace period would have ended in a SIGKILL first.

q: Which fix would you ship so that in-flight requests on keep-alive connections no longer delay the shutdown, without cutting them off?
options: Call server.closeAllConnections() as soon as SIGTERM arrives
Set keepAliveTimeout: 0 for the whole life of the server
Send Connection: close on responses written once shutdown has started, and keep a deadline that destroys leftovers
Raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 120 seconds
explain: The client closes the connection after its response, so the server closes as soon as the last request ends (25 ms on Express, 41 ms on Fastify, measured), and the deadline covers a stuck request. closeAllConnections() at once kills the requests you wanted to finish, and disabling keep-alive costs a new connection per request in normal operation.

q: A developer tries to run a Nest service without a build, using Node 24's type stripping: node src/main.ts. What happens?
options: It runs, but dependency injection fails at the first request
It fails to parse: type stripping does not run decorators, so the @ is a syntax error
It runs normally: Node 24 supports decorators natively
It runs only if reflect-metadata is imported first
explain: Measured on Node 24.11: SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token at @Injectable(). Nest also needs emitDecoratorMetadata, which only a compiler (tsc or SWC) can produce, so Nest projects keep a build step; reflect-metadata cannot help a file that does not parse.

q: Config uses @nestjs/config with PORT: z.coerce.number().int().default(3000). The deployment sets PORT= (empty). Which value does config.get('PORT') return?
options: 3000, because the variable is empty
The app refuses to start: an empty string is not a number
NaN, and listen throws
0, so the server would listen on a random free port
explain: Measured with @nestjs/config 12.0.1 and Zod 4.6.7: 0. Number('') is 0 and .default only applies to undefined. Drop blank values before validation (a small validate function) so an empty variable counts as missing.

q: A NestJS 12 app has no custom exception filter. A service throws new Error('connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432'). What does the client receive?
options: A 500 with the original error message in the body
A 500 with {"statusCode":500,"message":"Internal server error"}
A 500 with an application/problem+json body
A 503, because the error looks like a connection failure
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2 (Fastify adapter): Nest's built-in filter answers any unrecognised exception with that generic body. It does not leak the message, but it is not Problem Details either, so a global @Catch() filter calling toProblem is still the way to get one format.

q: A Nest app has a global ProblemFilter and a controller-level filter @Catch(OrderNotFoundError). The controller throws OrderNotFoundError. Which filters run?
options: Only the controller-level filter: the closest matching filter handles it and exceptions do not pass from filter to filter
Both, controller first, then global
Both, global first, then controller
Only the global filter, because global filters always win
explain: The Nest docs: filters are checked from route to controller to global, and a handled exception is not passed on to another filter. So a controller filter that answers differently silently bypasses the global Problem Details mapping, which is a good reason to keep one global filter.

q: The back-office routes of the Orders API only list, create and edit delivery zones, with no business rules. A colleague proposes ports, adapters and a use case per operation. What do you answer?
options: Agree: every service must follow hexagonal architecture to be testable
Agree, and also split it into three microservices to keep it clean
Refuse layering entirely and put SQL in the route handlers
Keep a thin controller over a repository; introduce use cases and ports when rules or external systems appear
explain: Ports pay off where there are rules to test without a database or external systems to replace. For plain CRUD they add files without protection; the layering still keeps SQL out of controllers, so rules can be added later without a rewrite.

q: A 12-person team wants to split its tangled orders monolith into four microservices to fix the coupling. What would you propose first?
options: Split now: separate deployables force clean boundaries
A modular monolith: modules with their own tables and a small public API, boundaries enforced in CI, and extraction later only for a scaling, deploy or ownership reason
Move all shared code into one common package used by every module
Put each module in its own repository so imports become impossible
explain: Splitting tangled code produces tangled services plus network failures and distributed transactions. Boundaries first, checked by a lint rule such as @nx/enforce-module-boundaries or dependency-cruiser, then extraction when one module really needs to scale or deploy separately; a big common package recreates the coupling.

q: The Orders API now lives in a monorepo with 30 packages and six teams. CI takes 40 minutes, and teams keep importing each other's internals. Which tooling addresses both problems?
options: pnpm workspaces alone, with pnpm -r test
One root tsconfig.json with path aliases
Nx: affected commands and caching for CI time, and the module boundary rule with project tags for the imports
Split into 30 repositories published to a private registry
explain: Nx caches and runs only affected tasks, and @nx/enforce-module-boundaries with depConstraints fails the lint when a project imports one it is not allowed to. pnpm workspaces alone link packages but neither cache nor enforce; Turborepo would cover caching but not the boundary rule.

q: A Dockerfile contains ENV STRIPE_API_KEY=sk_live_… "because the registry is private". What is the problem and the fix?
options: No problem: a private registry protects the image
The variable is only visible at build time, so the app cannot read it
Only the size: secrets should be compressed
The key persists in the image for everyone who can pull it; inject it at runtime from a secret manager and rotate the leaked key
explain: Docker's docs say build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for secrets because they persist in the final image. Anyone with pull access, every cache and every copy of the image now holds a live key, so it must be rotated, then provided at runtime by the platform.

q: What is the bug in this request-id middleware under real traffic?
options: Nothing, because Node runs JavaScript on one thread
Concurrent requests overwrite the shared variable, so logs written after an await carry another request's id; use AsyncLocalStorage
randomUUID is too slow to call per request
The middleware must be registered after the routes
explain: One thread does not mean one request at a time: while request A awaits the database, request B runs the middleware and overwrites the variable. AsyncLocalStorage.run gives each request its own store across awaits (measured with a pino mixin).

q: A Nest app on the Fastify adapter runs fine locally, but in its Docker container every request from outside fails to connect. main.ts calls await app.listen(3000). Likely cause?
options: Fastify listens on localhost by default; listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container
The Fastify adapter needs enableShutdownHooks() to accept connections
Port 3000 is reserved inside Docker containers
Nest needs the Express adapter in containers
explain: The Nest docs for the Fastify adapter: Fastify listens only on localhost by default, so pass '0.0.0.0' to accept connections from other hosts, which includes Docker's port mapping. Shutdown hooks only concern signals, and nothing reserves port 3000.

q: In a NestJS 12 app with enableShutdownHooks(), where do you close the PostgreSQL pool, and where do you fail readiness?
options: Both in onModuleDestroy, which runs after the server has closed
Pool in beforeApplicationShutdown, readiness in onApplicationShutdown
Fail readiness and wait in beforeApplicationShutdown (the server still serves); close the pool in onApplicationShutdown (after the server has closed)
Both in a process.on('SIGTERM') handler, since Nest hooks run after the process exits
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2 with both adapters: onModuleDestroy and beforeApplicationShutdown ran while a new connection still got 200, then the server closed, then onApplicationShutdown ran. Closing the pool before the server has drained breaks the requests still in flight.

q: With StandardSchemaValidationPipe registered globally, a client POSTs {"sku":"A","quantity":2,"extra":1}. What does the handler receive?
options: The raw body, including extra, since the pipe only validates
A 400 error, because extra is not in the schema
{ sku: 'A', quantity: 2 }: the schema's output, with the unknown key removed
An instance of a generated DTO class
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2: the handler received {"sku":"A","quantity":2} as a plain object. The pipe passes the schema's output by default (transform: true), and Zod objects strip unknown keys; a 400 would need z.strictObject.
